That was all the encouragement she needed.

“Well, my dear, Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been rented by a wealthy young man from the north of England. He came on Monday in a carriage drawn by four horses to inspect it, and liked it so much that he reached an agreement with Mr. Morris immediately. He'll move in before Michaelmas, and some of his servants will arrive by the end of next week.”

“What's his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Married or single?”

“Single, of course, my dear! A rich single man, with four or five thousand a year. How wonderful for our girls!”

“Why? What difference does it make to them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife replied, “how can you be so tiresome? You must realize I'm thinking of his marrying one of them.”

“Is that his reason for moving here?”

“His reason? Nonsense! How can you say such things? But he may very well fall in love with one of them, so you must visit him as soon as he arrives.”

“I see no need. You and the girls can go, or you might send them alone. That could be better, since you're as handsome as any of them and Mr. Bingley might prefer you to the others.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I certainly used to have my share of beauty, but I don't claim to be anything exceptional now. A woman with five grown daughters ought to stop thinking about her own looks.”

“A woman in that position doesn't usually have much beauty left to think about.”

“But, my dear, you really must call on Mr. Bingley when he moves into the neighborhood.”

“I certainly can't promise that.”

“Think of your daughters. Imagine what a fine home and position it would give one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to visit for that very reason, although, as you know, they don't normally call on newcomers. You must go, because we can't possibly visit him unless you do.”

“Surely you're too particular. I'm certain Mr. Bingley will be happy to see you. I'll send a note assuring him of my full consent to marry whichever of our daughters he chooses—though I must put in a good word for my little Lizzy.”

“I insist you do no such thing. Lizzy isn't any better than the others. She's certainly not half as beautiful as Jane, or half as good-tempered as Lydia.

“Goodbye, Uncle George. I'll be late for lunch if I stay longer. Thank you for telling me what I wanted to know. I always like to know everything about new friends and nothing about old ones.”

“Where are you eating, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha's. I've invited myself and Mr. Gray. He's the latest young person she's taken under her wing.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha to stop bothering me with requests for charity. I'm tired of them. She seems to think I have nothing to do but write checks for her silly projects.”

“All right, Uncle George. I'll tell her, but it won't help. People devoted to charity lose all feeling for human beings. That's their special quality.”

The old gentleman grunted approvingly and rang for his servant. Lord Henry walked through the low covered passage into Burlington Street and headed towards Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray's parents. Though crudely told, it had moved him, suggesting a strange, almost modern love story. A beautiful woman had risked everything for a wild passion. A few intense weeks of happiness had ended in a terrible, treacherous crime. Months of silent suffering followed, then a child born in pain. The mother died, leaving the boy alone under the harsh rule of an old man without love. Yes, it was an interesting background. It framed the boy, made him seem more perfect. Behind every beautiful thing lay something tragic. Worlds had to suffer birth pains for the smallest flower to open.... And how charming Dorian had been at dinner last night! He had sat across from him at the club, eyes wide with surprise, lips parted in a pleasure touched with fear. Red candle shades had deepened the pink of his face as wonder awakened in it. Talking to him was like playing a beautiful violin. He responded to every touch and movement of the bow.... Influencing someone was terribly fascinating. No other activity was like it. You could send your soul into another lovely form and let it stay a moment. You could hear your own ideas returned to you, made musical by youth and passion. You could pass your nature into someone else as if it were a delicate liquid or a strange perfume. There was real joy in that, perhaps the most satisfying joy still possible in their narrow, vulgar age, with its crude physical pleasures and ordinary ambitions.... The young man he had met by such a curious chance in Basil's studio was a wonderful example of humanity, too. Or at least he could be shaped into one.

She and the children could remain quite comfortably.”

“Ah, papa, you have never managed to arrange that, and I doubt you ever shall. Isabella cannot endure being left behind by her husband.”

The truth of this admitted no denial. However disagreeable, it drew only a resigned sigh from Mr. Woodhouse. Seeing his spirits sink at the thought of his daughter's devotion to her husband, Emma at once turned to an aspect of the matter certain to revive them.

“Harriet must favour us with as much company as possible while my sister and brother are here. She will certainly enjoy the children. We are very proud of them, are we not, papa? I wonder whether she will find Henry or John the handsomer.”

“Yes, I wonder which. Dear little creatures, how pleased they will be to arrive! They dearly love Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I am sure they do, sir. Indeed, I cannot think who does not.”

“Henry is a fine lad, but John much resembles his mother. Henry, the eldest, was called after me rather than his father. The second, John, bears his father's name. Some people, I believe, are surprised the eldest does not, but Isabella insisted upon Henry, which I found very sweet of her. He is a remarkably clever boy, too. They are all extraordinarily clever, and have so many charming little ways. They stand beside my chair and ask, ‘Grandpapa, may I have a piece of string?’ Once Henry requested a knife, but I explained that knives were made only for grandpapas. Their father, I think, is frequently too rough with them.”

“He seems rough to you,” Emma replied, “because you yourself are so gentle. If you could compare him with other fathers, you would judge him differently. He wants his sons to be energetic and hardy, and now and then he may speak sharply when they behave badly. But he is a loving father. Mr. John Knightley is certainly a loving father, and every one of the children is fond of him.”

“And then their uncle arrives and throws them up towards the ceiling in a most alarming fashion!”

“But they enjoy it, papa. Nothing pleases them better. They take such delight in it that, unless their uncle required them to have turns, the first would never surrender his place to the next.”

“Well, I cannot comprehend it.”

“We are all in that position, papa. Half the world cannot comprehend the other half's pleasures.”
